subject: rla
title: Inference and Textual Evidence
objectives: Students will distinguish between information a text states directly (explicit) and information it suggests (implicit).
Students will make reasonable inferences by combining text clues with everyday knowledge, and state them in their own words.
Students will choose the textual evidence that best supports an inference or claim, using the checks relevant, specific, and direct.
Students will infer a character's feelings, motives, and relationships from speech, actions, thoughts, and the reactions of others.
Students will recognize the common traps on inference questions: overreach, outside knowledge, contradicted, and true but irrelevant.
teach:
Lesson overview

Week 2 moves learners from what a text says to what a text means. On the GED Reasoning Through Language Arts (RLA) test, a large share of reading questions use words like infer, suggest, imply, and most likely, and many are followed by a second question that asks which evidence best supports the answer. This lesson teaches a simple, repeatable method: gather clues from the text, connect them with everyday reasoning, state a careful conclusion, and then prove it by pointing to the exact words. Tell learners early that an inference is not a guess. A good inference is the conclusion the text leads a careful reader to, and it can always be backed up with evidence.

Objectives

  • Tell the difference between information that is stated directly (explicit) and information that is suggested (implicit).
  • Make reasonable inferences by combining text clues with everyday knowledge.
  • Choose the piece of textual evidence that best supports an inference or claim.
  • Infer a character's feelings, motives, and relationships from speech, actions, thoughts, and reactions.
  • Recognize the four common traps on inference questions: overreach, outside knowledge, contradicted, and true but irrelevant.

Materials

  • Student Lesson (printed or on screen) and this week's Notes sheet
  • Whiteboard or shared screen; highlighters or markers in two colors (one for clues, one for conclusions)
  • Copies of the warm-up scene, the three worked-example texts, and the guided-practice passage (all included below)
  • A three-column organizer for each learner: Text clue | What I know | So I can infer
  • Week 2 practice items (the Calder Lake passage, items 1–5, are used for independent practice)

60-minute timing plan

SegmentMinutesWhat happens
Warm-up5“What happened here?” Learners infer from a described scene and list what they cannot know
Direct instruction20Stated vs. implied; the inference formula; the prove-it test; choosing the best evidence; inferring about characters; the four traps; three worked examples
Guided practice15Whole-group work on a short passage, five questions
Independent practice15Practice items 1–5 (Calder Lake passage); circulate and coach
Wrap-up5Checks for understanding; exit ticket; assign the week's study plan

Warm-up (5 minutes): What happened here?

Read this scene aloud or display it. Learners write one sentence that explains what happened, then list two things they cannot know from the scene.

You walk into a kitchen. On the counter is half of a chocolate cake with the number 7 written in blue frosting. Torn wrapping paper is stuffed into a trash bag by the door. Three balloons are tied to the back of a chair, and a stack of paper plates with smears of frosting sits next to the sink.

Answers (accept similar): A party for someone's seventh birthday took place here recently. Clues: the 7 on the cake, wrapping paper, balloons, used plates. Things we cannot know: the child's name, whether the child is a boy or a girl, how many guests came, whether everyone had a good time. Point out that both lists matter. The first list is an inference: it is not stated anywhere, but every clue points to it. The second list is where weak answer choices come from. A choice such as “The party was a surprise” might be true, but nothing in the scene proves it.

Direct instruction (20 minutes)

Talking point 1: Stated vs. implied (3 minutes)

Say: “When a text says something in so many words, the information is explicit, or stated directly. When the text gives you clues and expects you to put them together, the information is implicit, or implied. The author implies; the reader infers.” Write both verbs on the board with an arrow from author to reader. Learners often mix them up, and the GED uses both.

Talking point 2: The inference formula (3 minutes)

Write: Text clues + what I already know = inference. In the warm-up, the clues were the cake, paper, and balloons; what we already know is what birthday parties look like. Stress that the clues must come from the text. Everyday knowledge only connects the clues; it never replaces them. Hand out the three-column organizer and fill in one row from the warm-up together.

Talking point 3: The prove-it test (3 minutes)

Every correct inference on the GED can be proved by pointing to specific words. Teach learners to ask, for every answer choice: “Where does it say that, or what clues lead there?” If they cannot point to lines, the choice is out. A correct inference is often a small step from the text, not a big leap. If a choice needs a long chain of “maybe” to get there, it is probably wrong.

Talking point 4: Choosing the best evidence (4 minutes)

Many GED questions ask, “Which detail from the passage best supports…?” Several choices will be on the right topic. The best evidence passes three checks:

  • Relevant: it is about the exact claim, not just the same topic.
  • Specific: it gives a fact, number, action, or quotation, not a general statement.
  • Direct: if it is true, the claim must be true, or very nearly so. Weak evidence only makes the claim possible.

Tell learners that in a paired question, answering the first part carefully makes the second part easy: the evidence is usually the line that led them to the inference in the first place.

Talking point 5: Inferences about characters (3 minutes)

Fiction writers rarely say “she was nervous.” They show it. Teach four sources of clues: what a character says, what the character does, what the character thinks, and how others react to the character. Remind learners that characters do not always mean exactly what they say; a joke, a short answer, or a silence can carry meaning.

Talking point 6: The four traps (4 minutes, during the examples)

Wrong answers on inference questions usually fall into one of four traps. Name the trap aloud each time you eliminate a choice in the examples.

  • Overreach: goes further than the clues allow. Watch for extreme words such as all, never, always, only, proves.
  • Outside knowledge: might be true in real life, but the text does not support it.
  • Contradicted: the text actually says or shows the opposite.
  • True but irrelevant: a real detail from the text that does not answer the question asked.

Worked examples

Example 1: An inference from an informational paragraph

“When the Harbor Street Clinic began offering evening hours on Tuesdays and Thursdays, every appointment between 5 and 8 p.m. was booked within two days. Within a month, the share of patients who missed daytime appointments fell from 18 percent to 9 percent. Several patients told the staff they could not afford to take unpaid time off from work for a checkup.”

Question: Based on the paragraph, what can the reader infer? (a) Many patients had missed daytime appointments because they had to be at work. (b) The clinic will soon be open every evening of the week. (c) Evening appointments are less expensive than daytime appointments. (d) All of the clinic's patients prefer evening hours.

Solution. Step 1, gather clues: evening slots filled fast; daytime no-shows dropped by half; patients said they could not take unpaid time off. Step 2, connect them: if people stopped missing appointments once evening hours existed, and they said work was the problem, work was keeping them away. Step 3, prove it: the last sentence plus the drop in no-shows. Answer: (a). Choice (b) is overreach; nothing says the clinic plans more hours. Choice (c) is outside knowledge; cost is never mentioned. Choice (d) is overreach; the word all goes beyond the evidence.

Example 2: An inference about a character

“Marcus checked his phone for the fourth time in ten minutes. When the front door of the coffee shop opened, he stood up so fast that his chair scraped the floor. Then he saw it was only the mail carrier, and he sat back down slowly and smoothed the front of his new shirt.”

Question: What can the reader infer about Marcus?

Solution. Fill in the organizer together.

Text clueWhat I knowSo I can infer
Checks his phone four times in ten minutesPeople check often when they are waiting for somethingHe is waiting for someone or a message
Jumps up when the door opens; sits down slowly when it is the mail carrierDisappointment makes people slow downHe expected a specific person and was let down
Smooths his new shirtPeople dress up and fuss over clothes before something that mattersThe meeting is important to him

Inference: Marcus is nervously waiting to meet someone important to him. Ask learners what they cannot infer: who the person is (a date? a job contact?) or whether the person will arrive. An answer choice naming the exact person would be overreach.

Example 3: Choosing the best evidence

Claim: “The town's free tax-help clinic is meeting a real need in the community.” Which piece of evidence best supports the claim?

(a) “The clinic meets in the basement of the public library.” (b) “Tax forms have become more complicated over the years.” (c) “This year, volunteers helped 412 residents file their returns, and 90 more people were still on the waiting list when the season ended.” (d) “The clinic's director has volunteered there for ten years.”

Solution. Run the three checks on each choice. (a) is about the clinic but says nothing about need: true but irrelevant. (b) is general, not specific to this town, and it only makes a need possible. (d) shows the director's dedication, not the community's need. (c) is relevant (it measures demand), specific (412 and 90), and direct (more people wanted help than the clinic could serve). Answer: (c).

Guided practice (15 minutes)

Display the passage. Read it aloud once, then have learners reread it silently and mark clues in one color. Work through the questions together, asking a different learner to “prove it” each time.

The Pay-What-You-Can Shelf

For eleven years, Rosa Delgado has run Second Chapter Books on Mill Street. Last fall, she placed a wooden shelf by the front door with a hand-lettered sign: “Pay what you can. Take what you need.” Beside the shelf sits a coffee can with a slot cut in the lid. Delgado's accountant warned her that she would lose money. By spring, however, the can was collecting about as much each month as the shelf's books would have earned at their usual prices. Several regular customers began leaving bags of used books on the doorstep before the store opened. One of them, a bus driver named Curtis Bell, said he had not bought a book since high school. “Now I read on my breaks,” he said. “Some weeks I put in a dollar, and some weeks I put in five.” This spring, Delgado added a second shelf.

  1. What can you infer about how the shelf has worked out for Delgado? Expected: It has been a success. Proof: the can collects about what the books would normally earn, and she added a second shelf. Nobody expands something that is failing.
  2. Which detail best shows that the accountant's prediction was wrong? Expected: “By spring, however, the can was collecting about as much each month as the shelf's books would have earned at their usual prices.” Point out the signal word however.
  3. What can you infer about why customers leave bags of books on the doorstep? Expected: They support the shelf and want to keep it stocked. Clues: the donations are left by regular customers, they began after the shelf appeared, and a pay-what-you-can shelf needs a steady supply of books.
  4. What can you infer about Curtis Bell? Expected: The shelf helped him become a regular reader again, and he pays what he can manage. Proof: no books since high school, “Now I read on my breaks,” and the amount he pays changes from week to week. Push back if anyone says “He is poor”: that is overreach. We know only that his payment varies.
  5. Which statement is NOT supported by the passage: (a) Some customers value the shelf. (b) Delgado plans to close her store. (c) The shelf brings in about as much money as regular sales would. Expected: (b). Nothing suggests closing; adding a shelf suggests the opposite. Choice (c) is supported: the can collects about as much each month as the books would have earned at their usual prices.

Teacher note for independent practice: Assign practice items 1–5 (the Calder Lake passage). Ask learners to write the paragraph number of their proof next to each answer before checking. While circulating, ask “Where does it say that?” rather than “Is that right?” Learners who finish early may continue with items 6–8 (the short story).

Checks for understanding (wrap-up)

  1. What is the difference between imply and infer? Expected: the author or speaker implies (suggests); the reader infers (figures out).
  2. A choice says something that is probably true in real life but is not mentioned in the passage. Which trap is it? Expected: outside knowledge.
  3. Name the three checks for strong evidence. Expected: relevant, specific, direct.
  4. Name two ways a story shows what a character feels without saying it. Expected: any two of what the character says, does, or thinks, and how others react.
  5. Why should you be careful with an answer that uses the word always? Expected: extreme words often signal overreach, going beyond what the clues prove.

Common mistakes and how to correct them

Treating an inference as a guess. Learners pick any choice that could be true. Correction: require the prove-it test. If they cannot point to words in the text, the choice is out, no matter how reasonable it sounds.

Leaning on outside knowledge. A learner who knows a lot about a topic may choose what they know instead of what the text says. Correction: ask, “Would someone who knew nothing about this topic reach that answer from this passage alone?”

Overreaching. Learners take a reasonable idea one step too far, for example from “the shelf did well” to “Delgado will get rich.” Correction: circle extreme words and compare them with the strength of the clues.

Choosing evidence that is only on topic. The chosen detail mentions the right subject but does not prove the claim. Correction: have learners say, “If this detail is true, does the claim have to be true?”

Taking characters too literally. When a gruff character says, “Fix the coffee maker and you can stay forever,” learners may think he is making a real offer about coffee. Correction: ask what the character's tone and actions show, and how a real person would mean that line.

Differentiation

Support: Provide the sentence frame “The text says ____. I know that ____. So I can infer ____.” Start with one- or two-sentence texts and build to paragraphs. Let learners highlight clues before they read the answer choices. For multiple-choice items, have them cross out choices by trap name.

Stretch: Have learners write their own paired question for the guided-practice passage: one inference question and one “which evidence best supports” question, each with three wrong choices that represent different traps. Or give them two pieces of evidence for the same inference and have them argue which is stronger, using the three checks.

How this shows up on the GED

Inference and evidence questions appear throughout the RLA test, and the same skills are tested on Social Studies and Science. Typical wording includes:

  • “Based on the passage, it can be inferred that…”
  • “What does the author suggest about…?” or “The author implies that…”
  • “Which detail from the passage best supports the idea that…?”
  • “Why does the character most likely…?”
  • Paired items: a question about an inference followed by a question about the evidence for it.
  • Hot spot items: “Click the sentence that best supports…”
  • Drag-and-drop items that sort statements into “stated,” “inferred,” and “not supported.”

On the extended response, learners must also cite specific evidence from the passages. The habit built this week, making a point and then proving it with exact words, is the same habit that earns essay points. Learners will see these question types again in this week's Practice GED.
student:
Reading between the lines

Authors do not tell you everything. A news article may give you numbers and quotations but let you draw the conclusion. A story may never say that a character is scared; it shows her hands shaking. Figuring out what a text means but does not say is called making an inference. On the GED Reasoning Through Language Arts test, you will see many questions that ask what a passage suggests, what you can infer, or what a character would most likely do. Many of them come with a second question: which evidence best supports your answer?

Stated vs. implied

Stated (explicit)Implied (implicit)
What it meansThe text says it in so many words.The text gives clues and leaves the conclusion to you.
Example“Dana was angry.”“Dana slammed the door so hard that the pictures shook.”
Question wordsAccording to the passage…It can be inferred… The author suggests… most likely…

Imply or infer? The writer implies (hints). The reader infers (figures it out).

The inference formula

Text clues + what you already know = inference

The clues must come from the text. Your everyday knowledge is only the glue that connects them. For example, if a passage says a man came in with a dripping umbrella and wet shoes, you can infer that it is raining outside. The clues are the umbrella and shoes. What you know is that rain makes things wet.

Four steps for inference questions

  1. Read the question carefully. Note what it asks about: a person, an event, the author's view, a paragraph.
  2. Go back to the text. Find the part the question points to and mark the clues.
  3. Make your own inference first. Put the clues together in one sentence before you look at the choices.
  4. Prove it. Pick the choice that matches, and point to the words that support it. If you cannot point to words, the choice is wrong.

Choosing the best evidence

When a question asks which detail best supports an idea, several choices may be on the right topic. The best evidence is:

  • Relevant: about the exact idea, not just the same subject
  • Specific: a fact, number, action, or quotation
  • Direct: if the detail is true, the idea must be true, or very nearly so

Inferences about characters

In fiction, look at four kinds of clues: what a character says, what the character does, what the character thinks, and how other characters react. Also remember that people do not always say exactly what they mean. A joke, a short answer, or a silence can tell you a lot.

The four traps

TrapWhat it looks like
OverreachGoes further than the clues allow; often uses all, never, always, only
Outside knowledgeMight be true in real life, but the text does not support it
ContradictedThe text says or shows the opposite
True but irrelevantA real detail from the text that does not answer the question

Worked examples

Example 1: An informational text

A sign on a café door reads: “Starting Monday, we will close at 3 p.m. instead of 8 p.m. We are sorry for the inconvenience. We are hiring! Ask at the counter.”

What can you infer?

Step 1, clues: shorter hours; “We are hiring!” in the same notice. Step 2, connect: a business that needs workers and is cutting hours probably does not have enough staff to stay open late. Step 3, inference: The café is shortening its hours because it does not have enough workers. Step 4, check a trap: “The café is going out of business” is overreach. A business that is hiring is not closing.

Example 2: A character

“Jada read the email twice. Then she printed it, carried it to the kitchen, and taped it to the refrigerator right next to her son's spelling test with the gold star.”

What can you infer about the email?

Clue: she reads it twice (it matters to her). Clue: she prints it and displays it (people display things they are proud of). Clue: she places it next to a prize-winning test (another achievement). Inference: The email brought good news that Jada is proud of. You cannot infer exactly what the news was, such as a new job or a school acceptance. That would be overreach.

Example 3: The best evidence

Claim: “The town's new evening bus route is popular with riders.” Which detail best supports it?

(a) “The route runs from 6 p.m. to midnight.” (b) “Many people work evening shifts.” (c) “In its first month, the route carried 2,300 riders, twice what planners had predicted.” (d) “The new buses are painted green.”

Answer: (c). It is relevant (it measures how many people ride), specific (2,300; twice the prediction), and direct (high ridership means popular). Choices (a) and (d) are true but irrelevant. Choice (b) is general and only makes popularity possible.

Try it

1. “The Westside pool will open at 10 a.m. instead of 8 a.m. this week. Early-morning lap swim is canceled until we hire a second lifeguard.” What can you infer about the pool's staff right now?

Show answer

The pool does not have enough lifeguards, probably only one, to run the early-morning lap swim. Clue: the lap swim is canceled “until we hire a second lifeguard.”

2. “When the coach began reading the list of names, Ana stared at the floor and gripped the edge of the bench. When the coach reached the last name, Ana let out a long breath and grinned at her best friend.” What can you infer?

Show answer

Ana was worried she would not make the team, and she was relieved when she learned that she had made it. Clues: staring at the floor and gripping the bench show worry; the long breath and grin show relief.

3. Inference: “The repair shop has more work than it can handle.” Which detail best supports it? (a) “The shop opened in 2009.” (b) “Customers are now waiting three weeks for an appointment, and the owner has stopped taking new orders until January.” (c) “Car repairs can be expensive.”

Show answer

(b). It is relevant, specific, and direct: long waits and refused orders show the shop has more work than it can do. Choice (a) is true but irrelevant. Choice (c) is general and does not mention this shop.

4. “Mr. Ortiz looked at the dented fender, then at his teenage son, then back at the fender. ‘Well,’ he said, ‘I guess you found the mailbox.’” Which inference is best supported? (a) Mr. Ortiz thinks the damage is funny and does not care. (b) The son hit a mailbox with the car, and Mr. Ortiz is making a dry joke about it. (c) The son always drives carelessly.

Show answer

(b). The dented fender and the line about the mailbox point to an accident, and the remark is a dry joke rather than a literal statement. Choice (a) overreaches; a joke does not mean he does not care. Choice (c) uses always; one dent does not prove a pattern.
post:
Summary of key points

  • Information can be stated (explicit) or implied (implicit). The writer implies; the reader infers.
  • Text clues + what you already know = inference. The clues must come from the text.
  • An inference is not a guess. Use the prove-it test: point to the words that support your answer.
  • The best evidence is relevant, specific, and direct.
  • In fiction, infer from what characters say, do, and think, and how others react to them.
  • Avoid the four traps: overreach, outside knowledge, contradicted, and true but irrelevant.

Exit ticket

1. Fill in the blanks: A writer ____ an idea; a reader ____ it.

Show answer

A writer implies an idea; a reader infers it.

2. “Kenji's lunch sat untouched on his desk while he typed, deleted, and retyped the same sentence of his report.” What can you infer?

Show answer

Kenji is stressed or struggling with the report and is so focused on it that he has not eaten. Clues: untouched lunch; typing, deleting, and retyping the same sentence.

3. An answer choice says, “Every resident in the town supports the new park.” The passage quotes three residents who like the park. Which trap is this choice?

Show answer

Overreach. Three residents do not prove that every resident agrees.

4. What three checks make evidence strong?

Show answer

Relevant, specific, and direct.

5. Name four kinds of clues that help you infer what a character feels.

Show answer

What the character says, what the character does, what the character thinks, and how others react to the character.

Reflection

  • Think of a time this week when you figured out something no one told you directly, at work, at home, or from a text message. What clues did you use?
  • Which trap are you most likely to fall into? What will you do to catch it next time?
  • Was it easier to make inferences about real events or about story characters? Why?

This week's study plan

DayWhat to doTime
Day 1Reread the Student Lesson. Redo the Try it problems without looking at the answers.25 min
Day 2Study the vocabulary. Read one news article and write two inferences, each with the sentence that proves it.25 min
Day 3Complete practice items 1–5. For each one, write the paragraph number of your proof before checking.30 min
Day 4Complete practice items 6–12. For each miss, name the trap you fell into.30 min
Day 5Character drill: read a short story or a chapter of a novel. Fill in a Text clue | What I know | So I can infer chart for one character.25 min
Day 6Take this week's Practice GED for Reasoning Through Language Arts under timed conditions.40 min, continue on Day 7 if needed
Day 7Finish the Practice GED if needed. Review every missed question and list the skills to work on.30 min

Test-taking strategy: Prove it before you pick it

On any question with infer, suggest, or most likely, do not choose an answer until you can point to the words in the passage that support it. Put your finger (or your cursor) on the line. If you cannot find a line, cross the choice out. On paired questions, the line you pointed to for the first question is usually the answer to the second one.

vocab.def: A logical conclusion a reader reaches by combining clues in a text with everyday knowledge.
vocab.example: Wet shoes and a dripping umbrella lead to the inference that it is raining.

vocab.def: To figure out something that the text suggests but does not say directly. Readers infer.
vocab.example: From her shaking hands, I infer that she is nervous.

vocab.def: To suggest an idea without saying it directly. Writers and speakers imply.
vocab.example: By saying “We are hiring,” the sign implies the café needs workers.

vocab.def: Stated clearly and directly in the text.
vocab.example: “Dana was angry” states her feeling explicitly.

vocab.def: Suggested by clues but not stated directly.
vocab.example: Dana's anger is implicit in “She slammed the door.”

vocab.def: Specific words, facts, or quotations from a text that support an answer or claim.
vocab.example: “Ninety people were still on the waiting list” is textual evidence of high demand.

vocab.def: To point to or quote the exact part of a text that supports your answer.
vocab.example: Cite paragraph 4 to show that the ice now goes out earlier.

vocab.def: A detail in a text that helps the reader figure out something that is not stated.
vocab.example: Balloons and wrapping paper are clues that a party took place.

vocab.def: A judgment or decision reached by reasoning from evidence.
vocab.example: The shelf was a success, since the owner added a second one.

vocab.def: Backed up by evidence in the text; a supported answer can be proved by pointing to specific words.
vocab.example: “The pool is short on lifeguards” is supported by the canceled lap swim.

vocab.def: An answer that goes further than the evidence allows, often using words like all, never, always, or only.
vocab.example: “Everyone in town loves the park” overreaches if only three people are quoted.

vocab.def: The ways an author shows what a character is like, through speech, actions, thoughts, and others' reactions.
vocab.example: A boss who hands a new worker the store keys without a word shows trust.

vocab.def: A two-part GED question: the first asks for an inference, and the second asks which evidence best supports it.
vocab.example: Part A: What does the narrator suggest? Part B: Which sentence supports your answer?

notes:
Week 2 RLA Study Sheet: Inference and Textual Evidence

Key terms

  • Explicit: stated directly
  • Implicit: suggested by clues
  • Imply: what the writer does (hints)
  • Infer: what the reader does (figures out)
  • Inference: a conclusion supported by text clues
  • Textual evidence: exact words or facts that prove an answer

The formula

Text clues + what I know = inference

Clues come from the text. What you know only connects them.

Four steps

  1. Read the question; note what it asks about.
  2. Go back to the text; mark the clues.
  3. Make your own inference first.
  4. Prove it: point to the words.

Best evidence checklist

  • Relevant: about the exact idea
  • Specific: fact, number, action, or quote
  • Direct: if it is true, the idea must be true

Character clues

  • What the character says
  • What the character does
  • What the character thinks
  • How others react

People do not always mean exactly what they say. Read jokes and short answers for tone.

Prove-it test: If you cannot point to the words that support a choice, cross it out.

Answer traps

TrapSignAsk yourself
OverreachAll, never, always, only, provesDo the clues really go this far?
Outside knowledgeTrue in life, missing from the textCould I reach this from the passage alone?
ContradictedThe opposite of what the text showsDoes any line say otherwise?
True but irrelevantA real detail that does not answer the questionDoes this answer what was asked?

Question wording to recognize

“It can be inferred…” • “The author suggests…” • “most likely” • “Which detail best supports…?” • “Click the sentence that best supports…”

stimuli.title: The Day the Ice Goes Out
stimuli.html:
[1] Every spring for more than 140 years, someone in the town of Calder Lake has watched the water and waited. The moment they wait for is called “ice-out”: the day the lake is clear enough of ice that a boat could cross from the town dock to Gull Island. The first person to record the date was a ferry operator named Amos Whitlock, who began writing it inside the cover of his logbook in 1882. He had a practical reason. Until the ice went out, his ferry could not run.

[2] Whitlock's logbook now sits in a glass case at the Calder Lake Historical Society, and the tradition he started has never stopped. After he retired, the town's postmaster took over the job. Later it passed to a high school science teacher, and since 1998 it has belonged to a group of volunteers who take turns checking the lake each morning from late March until the ice is gone. The rule for declaring ice-out has never changed: a boat must be able to travel from the dock to the island without touching ice.

[3] For most of that history, the record was simply a piece of local trivia. Residents placed small bets on the date, and the winner's name appeared in the weekly newspaper. That changed in the early 2000s, when Dr. Nadia Ferro, a scientist at a nearby university, came across the logbook while researching a different project. “I almost walked past it,” she said. “Then I realized I was looking at one of the longest unbroken climate records in the region, kept by people who had no idea that was what they were doing.”

[4] Ferro and her students compared the dates decade by decade. In the 1880s, the ice went out, on average, on April 29. In the 2010s, the average was April 14. The change has not been steady. Some recent springs have been late, and a few early springs appear in the 1800s. But the overall direction is clear. Ferro notes that a single year tells you about weather, while a long record tells you about climate. “Any one date can fool you,” she said. “A hundred and forty dates are much harder to argue with.”

[5] Ice-out matters for more than boats. Fish such as lake trout depend on cold, oxygen-rich water, and the timing of the spring thaw affects when tiny organisms bloom in the lake, which in turn affects what young fish eat. Ray Ostrowski, who owns a bait shop near the dock, has noticed that ice fishing season, which once lasted well into March, now often ends weeks earlier. “Ten years ago, people were still buying ice augers from me in the middle of March,” he said. “Now I put them in storage by the end of February.”

[6] Ferro's team has since asked other towns to search their attics and archives for similar records. So far they have found eleven, including a church diary that noted when a river froze each winter and a mill owner's notes on when the millpond thawed. Not every record is usable. Some have gaps of many years, and some writers changed their rules for what counted as “frozen.” Ferro says that is exactly why the Calder Lake record is so valuable. “The same question, asked the same way, at the same spot, for 140 years,” she said. “You can't buy that. You can only inherit it.”

[7] The volunteers say the attention has not changed how they do the job. They still walk to the dock each morning with a notebook, and they still declare ice-out only when a boat could reach Gull Island without touching ice. One of them, a retired nurse named Ellen Pryce, keeps a yellowed newspaper clipping on her refrigerator. It reports that she won the town bet in 1987 with a guess of April 20. “I'd never win with that guess now,” she said, laughing.

stimuli.title: The Key Ring
stimuli.html:
An original short story.

[1] The bus let Teresa off a block early, so she walked the rest of the way past the laundromat and the empty shoe store, practicing under her breath. Good morning, Mr. Haddad. Thank you for this opportunity. I am a hard worker and a fast learner. She had repeated the words so many times on the ride that they had stopped sounding like words at all.

[2] Haddad Hardware smelled of sawdust and machine oil. Behind the counter, a gray-haired man with reading glasses pushed up on his forehead was sorting bolts into a metal tray. He did not look up when the bell over the door rang.

[3] “You're the one Delia sent,” he said.

[4] “Yes, sir. Teresa Lowe. Thank you for this—”

[5] “Can you cut a key?”

[6] She looked at the machine at the end of the counter, a squat gray box with two clamps and a grinding wheel. Her uncle had kept one exactly like it in the back of his garage, where she had spent most of the summer she turned twelve. “I haven't done it in a while,” she said.

[7] He slid a brass key across the counter without a word, then took a blank from a hook on the wall and set it beside the first. Teresa fastened both in the clamps, checked that their edges lined up, and tightened the knobs. Her hands seemed to remember before she did. The wheel whined, and a fine brass dust settled on her sleeve. When she was done, she ran her thumb along the new key's teeth, the way her uncle had shown her, found one rough spot, and smoothed it with a file before she handed the key back.

[8] Mr. Haddad held the two keys up to the window, side by side. He turned them over and held them up again. Then he put the old key in a drawer and dropped the new one into his own shirt pocket.

[9] He reached under the counter, brought out a ring holding four keys, and set it in front of her.

[10] “Front door, back door, register, storeroom,” he said. “I come in at seven. You open on Saturdays.” He went back to his bolts. “The coffee maker's broken. Fix that and you can stay forever.”

[11] Teresa closed her hand around the ring. It was heavier than it looked. She thought of the speech she had practiced on the bus and understood that she would never need to give it. Outside, a bus rumbled past the window, and for the first time in months, she did not check the time to see when the next one would come.

stimuli.title: Draft Notice: Boiler Replacement
stimuli.html:
To: All Residents of Linden Court Apartments
From: Building Management
Date: September 21
Subject: Boiler replacement on Tuesday, October 6

(1) Last January, our building's boiler broke down twice, and residents went without heat for a combined total of three days. After the second breakdown, the repair company told us that the boiler, which is 31 years old, could no longer be fixed reliably because (A) replacement parts are no longer made. (B) we have arranged to replace it before the cold weather returns.

(2) On Tuesday, October 6, the heat and hot water will be shut off from 8:00 a.m. to about 6:00 p.m. while the crew removes the old boiler and connects the new one. The laundry room will also be closed that day, because the washing machines use the building's hot water. Workers will need to reach the back wall of the basement storage area, so please move any items stored against the back wall of your storage unit by Monday evening, October 5.

(3) We understand that a day without hot water is an inconvenience. Any resident who has a medical need for hot water on October 6 should contact the office by Friday, October 2, so that we can make other arrangements. The community room on the first floor will stay open all day, and coffee and snacks will be provided.

(4) The new boiler is designed to use about 25 percent less gas than the old one. The savings from the new boiler's lower gas use (C) expected to help keep future rent increases small. Thank you for your patience as we make this improvement.

items.prompt: Based on paragraph 1, what can the reader infer about why Amos Whitlock recorded the ice-out date?
options: The date told him when he could begin earning money from his ferry again.
He was trying to measure how the region's climate was changing.
The town paid him to keep an official record of the lake.
He wanted to win the bet that residents placed on the date.
items.hint: Paragraph 1 says he had “a practical reason.” What could he not do until the ice went out?
items.explain:
Step 1. Find the clues. Paragraph 1 says Whitlock was a ferry operator, that he had “a practical reason,” and that “until the ice went out, his ferry could not run.”

Step 2. Connect them with what you know: a ferry operator earns money by running the ferry. If the ferry could not run until ice-out, the date marked when his work, and his income, could begin again.

Step 3. Match the choice: “The date told him when he could begin earning money from his ferry again.” Correct.

The climate choice is contradicted: paragraph 3 says the record keepers “had no idea” they were keeping a climate record. The payment choice is not supported; the passage never mentions pay. The bet choice is not supported; the bets are described in paragraph 3 and are never connected to Whitlock.

items.prompt: The reader can infer that ice-out on Calder Lake now usually comes earlier than it did in 1987. Click the sentence from paragraph 7 that best supports this inference.
spans: The volunteers say the attention has not changed how they do the job.
They still walk to the dock each morning with a notebook, and they still declare ice-out only when a boat could reach Gull Island without touching ice.
One of them, a retired nurse named Ellen Pryce, keeps a yellowed newspaper clipping on her refrigerator.
It reports that she won the town bet in 1987 with a guess of April 20.
“I'd never win with that guess now,” she said, laughing.
items.hint: One sentence tells you what happened in 1987. Which sentence tells you how things are different now?
items.explain:
Step 1. The inference compares two times: 1987 and now. The best evidence must say something about the present.

Step 2. The sentence before it tells us that in 1987, a guess of April 20 won the bet, so the ice went out around April 20 that year.

Step 3. Pryce says, “I'd never win with that guess now.” If April 20 would not win today, ice-out must now come on a different date, and paragraph 4 shows the trend is toward earlier dates (an average of April 14 in the 2010s). Correct.

The sentence about the 1987 bet is the main distractor. It gives the old date, but on its own it says nothing about today, so it cannot show a change. The first two sentences are about the volunteers' routine, which is true but irrelevant.

items.prompt: Based on Ray Ostrowski's statements in paragraph 5, what can the reader infer?
options: The ice on the lake is now thick enough for ice fishing during a shorter part of the year than it was ten years ago.
Fewer people in Calder Lake are interested in ice fishing than ten years ago.
Lake trout have disappeared from Calder Lake.
Ostrowski plans to stop selling ice fishing equipment.
items.hint: Ice fishing needs ice. Why would the season end earlier?
items.explain:
Step 1. Find the clues. Paragraph 5 says ice fishing season “once lasted well into March” and “now often ends weeks earlier.” Ostrowski used to sell ice augers (tools for drilling through ice) in mid-March but now stores them by the end of February.

Step 2. Connect them: ice fishing can happen only when the ice is solid. If the season ends weeks earlier, the ice is no longer solid as late into the year.

Step 3. The choice that says the ice is thick enough for ice fishing during a shorter part of the year matches. It also fits the passage's central point that the lake thaws earlier than it used to. Correct.

The interest choice is the main trap. It is not supported: the passage talks about the season ending earlier, which depends on the ice, and says nothing about how many people want to fish. The lake trout choice is overreach; paragraph 5 says only that the thaw affects what young fish eat. The choice about stopping sales is not supported; Ostrowski stores the augers, which suggests he will sell them again.

items.prompt: Dr. Ferro believes the Calder Lake record is especially valuable for studying climate. Which two details from the passage best support her view? Select two answers.
options: The rule for declaring ice-out has stayed the same since the record began.
The record has continued without a break for more than 140 years.
Residents placed small bets on the ice-out date each year.
Whitlock's logbook is displayed in a glass case at the historical society.
Some recent springs have had late ice-out dates.
A church diary recorded when a river froze each winter.
items.hint: Reread Ferro's quotation at the end of paragraph 6. What two qualities does she praise?
items.explain:
Step 1. Find Ferro's reasons. In paragraph 3 she calls it “one of the longest unbroken climate records.” In paragraph 6 she explains its value: “The same question, asked the same way, at the same spot, for 140 years.”

Step 2. Those words point to two qualities: the method never changed, and the record is long and unbroken.

Step 3. Match the choices. “The rule for declaring ice-out has stayed the same” (paragraph 2) shows the same method. “Continued without a break for more than 140 years” (paragraphs 1–3) shows length and no gaps. Both correct.

The bets and the glass case are true but irrelevant; they do not make the data more useful. Late recent springs are a detail that complicates the trend, not a reason the record is valuable. The church diary is a different record, and paragraph 6 suggests some of those records are less reliable.

items.prompt: In paragraph 4, Dr. Ferro says, “Any one date can fool you.” What does she most likely mean?
options: A single unusually early or late spring could give a false picture of the long-term pattern.
The volunteers sometimes record the wrong ice-out date.
Ice-out dates have no real connection to changes in climate.
The dates recorded in the 1880s are less accurate than recent dates.
items.hint: Read the sentences just before the quotation. What is the difference between weather and climate?
items.explain:
Step 1. Read the context. Just before the quotation, the author says some recent springs were late and some early springs appear in the 1800s, and that “a single year tells you about weather, while a long record tells you about climate.”

Step 2. Ferro follows with, “A hundred and forty dates are much harder to argue with.” She is contrasting one date with many dates.

Step 3. So “fool you” means that looking at one year, such as one late spring, could mislead you about the overall trend. The choice about a single unusually early or late spring giving a false picture is correct.

The wrong-date choice takes “fool” too literally; nothing suggests mistakes in the record. The no-connection choice is contradicted; Ferro says the long record shows a clear direction. The accuracy choice is not supported; the passage never questions the older dates.

items.prompt: Based on paragraphs 1 and 4, how does Teresa most likely feel as she arrives at Haddad Hardware?
options: nervous and eager to make a good impression
confident because she has worked at the store before
irritated that the bus let her off a block early
unsure whether she wants the job at all
items.hint: What is she doing as she walks, and how many times has she done it?
items.explain:
Step 1. Gather clues about what Teresa does and says. In paragraph 1 she practices a speech “under her breath” and has repeated it “so many times” that the words have lost their meaning. In paragraph 4 she politely starts her prepared thank-you: “Yes, sir… Thank you for this—”

Step 2. Connect them: people rehearse over and over when they are anxious about something that matters to them, and a prepared, polite greeting shows she wants to make a good impression.

Step 3. “Nervous and eager to make a good impression” fits. Correct.

The confident choice is contradicted: Mr. Haddad identifies her only as “the one Delia sent,” so they are meeting for the first time and she has not worked there before. The irritated choice is not supported; the story mentions the early stop but shows no annoyance. The unsure choice is contradicted by all her preparation.

items.prompt: Mr. Haddad never says, “You're hired.” Which detail from the story best supports the inference that he has decided to hire Teresa?
options: He gives her a ring of store keys and tells her she will open the store on Saturdays.
He holds the two keys up to the window, side by side.
He asks her, “Can you cut a key?”
He does not look up when the bell over the door rings.
items.hint: Which action would a boss take only after deciding to trust a new worker?
items.explain:
Step 1. The inference is that he has decided to hire her. The best evidence must show a decision, not just a test.

Step 2. Check each choice. Holding the keys to the window shows him checking her work, before any decision. Asking “Can you cut a key?” starts the test. Not looking up shows his gruff manner, which is true but irrelevant.

Step 3. Handing her the keys to the front door, back door, register, and storeroom and saying, “You open on Saturdays,” only makes sense if she now works there. It is relevant, specific, and direct. Correct.

items.prompt: Drag each statement into the correct category based on the story.
choices: Teresa's uncle kept a key-cutting machine in his garage.
Mr. Haddad comes in to the store at seven.
Teresa had cut keys before, years earlier.
Mr. Haddad is satisfied with the key Teresa made.
Teresa will earn more than the store's other workers.
items.hint: For each statement, ask: Does the story say this in so many words? If not, do the clues lead there? If not, it is not supported.
items.explain:
Stated directly: “Her uncle had kept one exactly like it in the back of his garage” (paragraph 6). “I come in at seven” (paragraph 10). Both are said in so many words.

Reasonable inference: The story never says Teresa cut keys before, but she says, “I haven't done it in a while,” she spent a summer in her uncle's garage near the same kind of machine, and “her hands seemed to remember.” The story never says Mr. Haddad is satisfied, but he checks the key twice, puts it in his own pocket, and then hands her the store keys.

Not supported: The story names Delia only as the person who sent Teresa; nothing says how she is related to Mr. Haddad. Pay is never mentioned. These are guesses, not inferences.

items.skill: Frequently confused words; transitions; subject-verb agreement
items.prompt:
Read the draft notice. Then choose the option that correctly completes each blank in these excerpts.

Paragraph 1, blank (A): …the boiler, which is 31 years old, could no longer be fixed reliably because {{0}} replacement parts are no longer made.

Paragraph 1, blank (B): {{1}} we have arranged to replace it before the cold weather returns.

Paragraph 4, blank (C): The savings from the new boiler's lower gas use {{2}} expected to help keep future rent increases small.

options: its
it's
its'
their
For this reason,
However,
For example,
On the other hand,
are
is
was
being

items.hint: (A): Which word shows that the parts belong to the boiler? (B): Is the replacement a result of the breakdowns, a contrast, or an example? (C): Find the main noun of the subject. Is it singular or plural?
items.explain:
Blank (A). Step 1: The parts belong to the boiler, so a possessive is needed. Step 2: The possessive of it is its, with no apostrophe. Correct. “It's” means it is (“because it is replacement parts” makes no sense). “Its'” is not a word. “Their” is plural, but boiler is singular.

Blank (B). Step 1: The sentences before it say the boiler broke twice and could not be fixed reliably. Step 2: Replacing it is the result of those problems. Step 3: A cause-and-effect transition is needed: “For this reason.” Correct. “However” and “On the other hand” signal a contrast, and “For example” introduces an example, but the replacement is neither.

Blank (C). Step 1: Find the subject. In “The savings from the new boiler's lower gas use,” the main noun is savings; “from the new boiler's lower gas use” only describes it. Step 2: Savings is plural. Step 3: The notice describes a current expectation in the present tense, so the plural present verb is needed: “The savings… are expected.” Correct. “Is” is singular; it would agree with the nearby word use, which is a common trap. “Was” is singular and past tense. “Being” cannot be the main verb and would leave a fragment.

items.prompt: Based on the notice, which resident would most likely need to contact the building office by Friday, October 2?
options: a resident who must soak in warm water each day as part of a treatment ordered by a doctor
a resident who usually does laundry in the building on Tuesdays
a resident who keeps boxes against the back wall of a basement storage unit
a resident who works from home and will need heat during the day
items.hint: Find the sentence in the notice that mentions Friday, October 2. Who does it ask to contact the office?
items.explain:
Step 1. Find the request. Paragraph 3 says: “Any resident who has a medical need for hot water on October 6 should contact the office by Friday, October 2.”

Step 2. Apply it. A daily warm-water soak ordered by a doctor is a medical need for hot water, and the hot water will be off on October 6. This resident fits the request. Correct.

The storage-unit choice is the main trap. That resident does need to act, but paragraph 2 asks them to move items by Monday evening, not to contact the office. The laundry resident is affected, but the notice asks nothing of them; they can simply do laundry another day. The work-from-home resident will lose heat, but the notice asks only residents with a medical need for hot water to contact the office, and it offers the community room to everyone.

items.prompt: In paragraph 10, Mr. Haddad says, “The coffee maker's broken. Fix that and you can stay forever.” What does this remark most likely suggest about him?
options: He shows his approval through dry humor rather than direct praise.
He hired Teresa mainly so that she could repair the store's equipment.
He is angry that no one has fixed the coffee maker.
He doubts that Teresa will stay at the job for very long.
items.hint: Has Mr. Haddad praised Teresa directly anywhere in the story? How does he show what he thinks instead?
items.explain:
Step 1. Look at how Mr. Haddad acts throughout the story. He does not look up when she enters, cuts her off mid-sentence, and slides the key over “without a word.” He never says “good job” or “you're hired.” Instead, he shows approval through actions: pocketing her key and handing her the store keys.

Step 2. Read the line for tone. “Stay forever” over a coffee maker is an exaggeration. Coming right after he gives her the keys, it reads as a joke, a gruff man's way of saying he is pleased with her.

Step 3. “He shows his approval through dry humor rather than direct praise.” Correct.

The repair choice overreaches: he hired her after she cut a key, and the coffee maker is mentioned only as a joke. The angry choice is not supported; nothing in his words or actions shows anger. The doubt choice is contradicted; “stay forever” and the keys suggest he expects her to stay.

items.prompt: In paragraph 6, the author explains that some other records “have gaps of many years” and that “some writers changed their rules for what counted as ‘frozen.’” What is the most likely reason the author includes this information?
options: to show, by contrast, why the unbroken, consistent Calder Lake record is so valuable
to argue that all eleven of the other records should be thrown out
to suggest that Dr. Ferro's findings about Calder Lake may not be reliable
to explain why church diaries are more trustworthy than a mill owner's notes
items.hint: Read the sentence that comes right after these details. What does Ferro say is “exactly why” Calder Lake's record is valuable?
items.explain:
Step 1. Read the details in context. Right after them, the author writes, “Ferro says that is exactly why the Calder Lake record is so valuable,” and Ferro describes it as “the same question, asked the same way, at the same spot, for 140 years.”

Step 2. Connect the ideas. Gaps and changing rules are the weaknesses of the other records. Paragraph 2 told us that Calder Lake's record never stopped and its rule never changed. The weaknesses of the other records make Calder Lake's strengths stand out.

Step 3. The author includes these details to show the contrast. The choice that says the author shows, by contrast, why the Calder Lake record is so valuable is correct.

The thrown-out choice overreaches: the passage says “not every record is usable,” not that none are, and all is an extreme word. The reliability choice is contradicted; the details make the Calder Lake record look stronger, not weaker. The church diary choice is not supported; the passage never compares those two records.
